audit_status.source_base: Hebrew 1 Chronicles / Divrei Hayamim Aleph Rabbah conquest and Philistine champion traditions, first-pass restored draft with public-domain scaffold; later witness audit required
audit_status.review_note: Reviewed against 2 Samuel 11-12 and 21 for omitted Bathsheba/Uriah narrative, Rabbah siege and spoil, v3 forced-labor/execution ambiguity, crown imagery, giant/champion terminology, Goliath/Lahmi textual relationship, stature and polydactyly, and Philistine reception.

verses.restored: At return of year, at time kings go out, Joab led army power, devastated land of Ammonites, came and besieged Rabbah. David remained in Jerusalem. Joab struck Rabbah and tore it down.
David took crown of their king/Milcom from his head; its weight was found a talent of gold with precious stone, and it was set on David's head. He brought very much spoil from city.
He brought out people in it and set/cut them with saws, iron picks/harrows, and axes; thus David did to all cities of Ammonites. David and all people returned to Jerusalem.
After this war arose at Gezer with Philistines; Sibbecai the Hushathite struck Sippai from descendants of Rephaim, and they were subdued.
Again there was war with Philistines; Elhanan son of Jair struck Lahmi brother of Goliath the Gittite, whose spear shaft was like weaver's beam.
Again there was war at Gath, where there was a man of great measure with six fingers on each hand and six toes on each foot, twenty-four; he also was descended from Rephaim.
He taunted Israel, and Jonathan son of Shimea, David's brother, struck him.
These were born to Rephaim in Gath, and they fell by hand of David and hand of servants.

translation_notes: Chronicles omits David's sexual abuse of Bathsheba, Uriah's command murder, and Nathan's confrontation, although verse 1 occupies the same campaign setting. The omission must not rehabilitate David through silence.
Joab devastates Ammonite land and destroys Rabbah; civilians, homes, food systems, and grief remain behind the royal summary.
The crown and extensive spoil are trophies of conquest. Sacred or royal display does not legitimate plunder.
Verse 3 is textually and ethically difficult: it may describe killing/torture with tools or placing people into forced labor using those tools. Neither reading is benign.
Ammonite captives are people, not labor inventory or objects for exemplary cruelty.
Rephaim and 'great stature' language describe ancient champion traditions, not monsters, demons, or inferior bodies.
Six fingers and toes is polydactyly, a human bodily variation; it is not a sign of evil, giant blood, or spiritual threat.
The Goliath/Lahmi wording differs across Samuel and Chronicles and requires close textual audit.
Philistine champions remain human opponents and may not become modern ethnic stereotypes.
safety_note: Do not let Chronicles' omission erase Bathsheba and Uriah. Reject torture, forced labor, plunder, disability stigma, polydactyly superstition, giant mythology used against real bodies, and anti-Philistine hatred. Rabbah's conquered people remain the chapter's most endangered community.
